Market Overview

🌎 One of the busiest weeks in the sector for a while, and a deep dive into how NASA has turned to lucrative selected contractors for their advancement

SpaceX attempted the first full two stage recovery of a Starship vehicle on Friday night, NASA opened its checkbook for a wave of Moon Base contracts worth well over a billion dollars combined, and Q3 earnings season hit the space sector in earnest, with Rocket Lab, AST SpaceMobile, Spire Global, Firefly Aerospace and Virgin Galactic all reporting. The net effect: a sector that spent most of the year trading on launch cadence and AI-adjacent enthusiasm is now also being priced on backlog quality and lunar program exposure.


SpaceX (SPCX)

SpaceX shares jumped 5.8% on Monday, November 9, after NASA named eight companies, including SpaceX, Blue Origin and Intuitive Machines, to compete for up to $10 billion (potentially $15 billion with a five year option) in new Commercial Lunar Payload Services 2 contracts as part of a broader package NASA described as roughly $1.3 billion in initial Moon Base awards for landers, rovers and drones. The bigger event of the week came Friday evening: SpaceX launched Starship Flight 15 at 5:45 p.m. ET on November 13 in its first attempt to recover both the Super Heavy booster and the Ship upper stage in the same mission. The booster aborted its "chopsticks" catch roughly 6.5 minutes after liftoff following a guidance and propellant issue (Musk said the Raptor engines slightly underperformed) and its flight termination system triggered a loss over the Gulf of Mexico. Ship 42 fared better: it reached a 275 km orbit, deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, completed roughly 14 orbits, and was caught by the launch tower back at Starbase on Saturday, November 14, becoming the first orbital rocket upper stage ever returned to and caught at its launch site. Shares were broadly unaffected by the mixed outcome, with analysts framing the ship catch as the harder and more commercially important milestone. Separately, SpaceX's next major insider lockup tranche is not due until well into 2027 (Musk's own shares are locked until June 2027), with the last large unlock having cleared in August; investors should treat any near term short interest figures with caution given how quickly they have moved over the past two quarters.

Rocket Lab (RKLB)

Rocket Lab reported Q3 2026 results on Monday, November 9: record quarterly revenue of $268 million, up 73% year over year, and a record backlog of $3.57 billion after a $1.2 billion sequential jump. The company also disclosed more than $515 million in new Neutron launch deals signed with constellation operators during the quarter, alongside a per-mission Neutron price increase. Shares still fell more than 5% after the print, as a GAAP net loss came in worse than modeled and management acknowledged further schedule pressure on Neutron's maiden launch, now expected to slip into 2027.

AST SpaceMobile (ASTS)

AST SpaceMobile posted Q3 2026 revenue of $42.3 million, up 187% year over year, in a business update issued November 10. Management reiterated a target of nationwide intermittent direct to device service in the U.S. by year end, while flagging continued heavy capital spending tied to BlueBird satellite production and a roughly $4 billion debt load. The company also disclosed it is developing its own 20 ton class rocket to deploy BlueBird satellites, using Miranda engines supplied by Firefly Aerospace.

Intuitive Machines (LUNR)

Intuitive Machines was one of eight companies NASA named on November 9 to compete for the new CLPS 2 lunar delivery vehicle, a multiple award contract with a combined ceiling of $10 billion across all winners (up to $15 billion if NASA exercises a five year option), covering roughly a decade of task orders spanning full payload delivery missions, lander acquisitions, surface mobility and lunar night survival work. CEO Steve Altemus said the award helps "accelerate NASA's Moon Base initiative." The CLPS 2 vehicle sits alongside, not in place of, the company's existing Nova C and Nova D lander contracts.

Virgin Galactic (SPCE)

Virgin Galactic reported Q3 2026 results after the close on November 12: revenue of $0.4 million, in line with estimates, a GAAP loss per share of $0.50, and a net loss of $58.8 million, against a cash position of $184 million. The lead Delta class spaceship, Apeiron, has now arrived at Spaceport America, with a first glide flight targeted for January 2027. Management pushed its first commercial spaceflight target to early Q2 2027, a further slip from prior guidance, with a second ship not expected to begin commercial service until late Q2 or early Q3 2027. Shares slid in the sessions after the print on the delay and ongoing cash burn.

Spire Global (SPIR)

Spire Global announced Q3 2026 results on November 10: revenue of $18.0 million, up 42% year over year (77% excluding the maritime business it is exiting), alongside two new NOAA awards totaling $61.2 million in base value, a $33.2 million GNSS radio occultation data task order that could reach roughly $66 million with unfunded surge options, and a $28 million hyperspectral microwave sounding contract. Management guided full year 2026 revenue to $75 to $80 million and gave preliminary 2027 revenue guidance of $96 to $106 million.

Redwire (RDW)

Redwire was awarded a roughly $40 million contract on November 10 by NASA's Moon Base Infrastructure Office to adapt its flight proven Roll Out Solar Array technology into an integrated lunar power generation demonstration near the south pole, covering vertically deployed solar arrays, batteries and wireless power transfer hardware. Redwire Space president Mike Gold called Moon Base "one of the most important human spaceflight initiatives for America since Apollo." The award came days after the eighth and final Redwire built ROSA wing was installed on the International Space Station.

Viasat (VSAT)

Viasat was named on November 9 as one of three companies, alongside SES and Astranis, selected for Phase 1 of NASA's NEXUS initiative, winning a contract valued up to $460.9 million as part of roughly $1.1 billion NASA is committing across the three awardees for Ka band space relay services that will eventually replace elements of the agency's aging Near Space Network and support direct to Earth communications for lunar missions.

Planet Labs (PL)

Planet Labs signed a multi launch agreement with Stoke Space on November 9 covering future satellite deployments on Stoke's reusable Nova rocket, continuing Planet's strategy of diversifying its launch provider base beyond its traditional rideshare arrangements.

Globalstar (GSAT)

France's spectrum regulator authorized Globalstar on November 10 to launch and operate 54 next generation direct to device satellites under a 20 year license, extending the U.S. FCC authorization for the same C-3 system granted in October. The approval is incremental progress toward the buildout Amazon is funding as part of its pending $11.57 billion acquisition of Globalstar, announced earlier this year.

Firefly Aerospace (FLY)

Firefly Aerospace reported Q3 2026 results on November 10: revenue surged 259% year over year to $111 million, and the company disclosed a record backlog of $1.7 billion. Shares initially rallied on the beat, with Deutsche Bank reiterating upside, though some coverage noted the stock's rally stalled even as losses widened alongside the revenue growth.

Takeaway

This was the week the space sector's two biggest narratives, reusability economics and lunar infrastructure spending, openly merged. NASA did not simply announce a Moon Base program; it wrote checks across landers (Intuitive Machines), power generation (Redwire), and communications relays (Viasat), with SpaceX also in the mix as a CLPS 2 competitor. Layered on top, SpaceX's partial success on Flight 15 is a reminder that the reusability bet underpinning Starlink V3 economics, and ultimately Artemis tanker flights, is still being proven out one mission at a time. Into next week, watch for follow through commentary on Rocket Lab's Neutron timeline, any additional NEXUS Phase 2 signals, and whether Virgin Galactic's further flight delay draws analyst downgrades.

🎯NASA'S MOON BASE PUSH JUST TURNED A DOZEN SMALL CAPS INTO LUNAR CONTRACTORS

The Nov. 9 announcement, in dollars

On Monday, November 9, NASA put a number on its lunar ambitions that the space equity market had been waiting on for months. The agency named eight companies, SpaceX, Blue Origin, Intuitive Machines and five others, as eligible competitors for its next generation Commercial Lunar Payload Services vehicle, CLPS 2, a multiple award, indefinite delivery contract with a combined ceiling of $10 billion across all winners. NASA structured in a five year option that, if exercised, could push the total ceiling to $15 billion. Trade press framed the headline figure as roughly $1.3 billion in near term Moon Base awards once landers, rovers and drones awarded the same day were totaled, a mix of firm task orders and ceiling commitments that will be parceled out over what NASA describes as a decade long procurement window.

That same morning, NASA separately confirmed roughly $1.1 billion committed across three companies, Viasat, SES and Astranis, for Phase 1 of its NEXUS initiative: Ka band space relay services meant to eventually succeed parts of the aging Near Space Network and support direct to Earth links for lunar missions. Viasat's individual award was disclosed at up to $460.9 million. A day later, Redwire picked up a roughly $40 million NASA Moon Base Infrastructure Office award to adapt its Roll Out Solar Array technology for an autonomous lunar power demonstration near the south pole.

Who actually got paid this week, not just named

The distinction matters because being named a CLPS 2 competitor is not the same as being awarded a task order, and several headlines this week blurred the two. Intuitive Machines was named to the CLPS 2 vehicle, a multi year eligibility designation, not a dollar figure delivered this week. By contrast, Redwire's $40 million award and Viasat's up to $460.9 million NEXUS Phase 1 contract are real, obligated dollars tied to specific statements of work with near term deliverables: an integrated power demonstration near the lunar south pole for Redwire, and Ka band relay development for Viasat. SpaceX, also named to CLPS 2 alongside Blue Origin, saw its stock pop 5.8% that Monday less on any single contract and more on the market reading the announcement as confirmation that NASA intends to spread Moon Base dollars across a wide bench of contractors rather than consolidating around one or two primes.

The relay contracts most coverage filed under a different story

The NEXUS awards deserve more attention than they got relative to the lander headlines. NASA's existing space communications infrastructure, built mostly around an aging network of relay satellites and ground stations, was never designed for a sustained lunar presence with multiple simultaneous surface and orbital assets. The agency's decision to split $1.1 billion in Phase 1 funding across three companies, rather than a single prime, mirrors the CLPS model: breed competition early, award follow on task orders to whichever teams demonstrate working hardware fastest. For Viasat, a company whose core consumer and government satcom businesses have faced pricing pressure for several quarters, a confirmed NASA relationship with a near half billion dollar ceiling is a meaningfully different kind of revenue than another broadband capacity deal.

Why the market is treating this as more than routine news flow

Space equity investors have watched government lunar spending headlines come and go for several years without much follow through on actual obligated dollars. What changed this week is specificity: named dollar ceilings, named task areas (power, relay, delivery), and a same week cluster of three separate announcements touching five of the thirteen companies this newsletter tracks. Analysts covering Intuitive Machines and Redwire in particular pointed to the CLPS 2 ceiling and the ROSA demonstration award as evidence that NASA's Moon Base initiative is shifting from planning documents into executable task orders, a distinction that matters for how these companies get valued. A $10 billion ceiling split across eight competitors is not $1.25 billion of guaranteed revenue per company; it is closer to a qualification round, with real money following only as task orders get issued against specific milestones over the coming decade.

What has to go right from here

Three things will determine whether this week's announcements translate into durable revenue rather than one time headlines. First, NASA's own budget: Moon Base funding competes with Artemis crewed lunar lander spending and broader agency priorities that have faced congressional scrutiny in recent budget cycles. Second, execution: Redwire's ROSA demonstration and Viasat's NEXUS relay work both involve hardware that has to perform in the harsh thermal and radiation environment of the lunar surface or cislunar space, with no guarantee of success on first attempts, as this week's mixed Starship Flight 15 outcome at SpaceX illustrates for the sector generally. Third, the task order cadence: CLPS 2 winners will not know their actual share of the $10 to $15 billion ceiling until NASA starts issuing individual task orders, likely over the next 12 to 18 months, and early task orders have historically gone disproportionately to whichever contractor has flight proven hardware ready first, a dynamic that currently favors Intuitive Machines given its existing Nova C and Nova D lander heritage.

Takeaway

This week turned NASA's Moon Base rhetoric into a specific, multi company contracting program with real dollar ceilings attached, spreading exposure across lander delivery (Intuitive Machines, alongside SpaceX and Blue Origin), surface power (Redwire), and orbital relay communications (Viasat). The distinction between "named as eligible" and "awarded a task order" will matter enormously for how quickly these contracts show up in quarterly revenue, and investors should expect the next 12 to 18 months of individual task order announcements, rather than this week's ceiling figures, to be the real signal on which companies actually benefit.
